paper_sections.title: Arithmetic in two languages: Localizing simple multiplication processing in the adult bilingual brain

description.value: The study examined whether simple multiplication processing differs between the language in which bilingual adults learned multiplication and their other language, using behavioral measures and fMRI, with language and problem-size effects assessed in language- and quantity-related regions.

design.value: Thirty-five Spanish-English bilingual adults were recruited; six were excluded and the final sample comprised 29 participants. Participants completed two localizer tasks and a single-digit multiplication verification task during one fMRI session. The verbal localizer and multiplication task were administered in English and Spanish, with language order alternated across participants; the numerosity localizer was administered in two runs.

description.value: Test 14: Picture Vocabulary, Test 15: Oral Comprehension, and Test 8: Incomplete Words were used to measure English vocabulary, language comprehension, and phonological awareness.
Equivalent Spanish versions of the language proficiency tests were administered.
Aged-normalized classifications were obtained from raw assessment scores in each language and compared across parallel subtests.

task_description.value: Participants heard two spoken number words, followed by a visual Arabic digit, and determined whether the Arabic digit was the correct product of the two spoken numbers. They used their index finger if the proposed solution was true and their middle finger if the proposed solution was false.

instructions.value: Participants were instructed to determine whether the Arabic digit was the correct product of the two spoken numbers.

stimuli.value: Spoken number words in English or Spanish followed by a visual Arabic digit; all words were normalized to 450 ms in duration.

instructions.value: Participants determined whether the spoken word matched the presented picture or not.

instructions.value: Participants were tasked with determining which of two sequentially presented dot arrays contained more dots.

description.value: Before functional image acquisition, a high-resolution T1-weighted 3D structural image was acquired for each participant.

Functional images were realigned, anatomical images were skull-stripped using segmentation products, functional images were co-registered to the skull-stripped anatomical image, normalized to the standard T1 Montreal Neurological Institute template, smoothed with a 6 mm isotropic Gaussian kernel, and motion outlier volumes were identified and repaired.

steps.value: all functional images were realigned to their mean functional image across runs

an anatomical brain mask was created by combining the segmentation products (i.e., grey matter, white matter, and cerebrospinal fluid), and then applied to its original anatomical image to produce a skull-stripped anatomical image
the mean functional image and all functional images were co-registered to the skull-stripped anatomical image
all the functional images were normalized to the standard T1 Montreal Neurological Institute (MNI) template
smoothing was applied to all the functional images with a 6 mm isotropic Gaussian kernel
Art-Repair was used to identify outlier volumes
Outlier volumes were repaired by interpolation between the nearest non-outlier volumes.
Six motion parameters estimated during realignment were entered in the first-level modeling as regressors, and the repaired volumes were deweighted.

model_settings.value: Activation was modeled as epochs with onsets time-locked to the presentation of the first stimulus in each trial. All epochs were convolved with a canonical hemodynamic response function. The time series data were high-pass filtered (1/128 Hz), and serial correlations were corrected using an autoregressive AR model. Six motion parameters were entered as regressors; repaired volumes were deweighted.
Subjects were included as a random effect; Satterthwaite’s method was used to estimate denominator degrees of freedom for F statistics.

estimator.value: generalized linear model from the lme4 package in R

model_settings.value: Brain data were modeled based on Problem Size, Language, and the additive effect with and without the interaction between the two. The Watanabe information criteria comparison (WAIC) was used to determine which model best fit the data, and posterior summaries provided Bayesian p-values.
